claims.text: The initial material is conventional austenitic stainless steel, such as 316L, with a standard mill finish.
Plasma nitriding at approximately 400–500 °C in a controlled ammonia or nitrogen-rich atmosphere is an appropriate surface treatment for the stainless steel.
Controlled-temperature plasma nitriding will form a nitrogen-enriched diffusion layer on austenitic stainless steel.
The nitrogen-enriched layer is S-phase, also described as expanded austenite.
The nitrogen-enriched surface layer enhances passivity.
The nitrogen-enriched surface layer reduces pitting-initiation sites.
During plasma nitriding, nitrogen atoms diffuse into the steel surface lattice.
Interstitial nitrogen diffusion creates a modified surface microstructure.
The modified microstructure lowers the diffusion rates of corrosive species.
The modified microstructure increases the stability of the surface passivation layer.
Plasma-nitrided stainless steel will have significantly better corrosion resistance in aggressive aqueous environments than untreated stainless steel.
Under the specified acidic or chloride-rich conditions, nitriding will lower mass-loss corrosion rates by at least 20–30% relative to untreated stainless steel.
The predicted protection applies to chloride-rich or acidic solutions at approximately 50–80 °C for exposure durations of up to 500 hours.
Enhanced corrosion resistance is most reliable only within particular plasma-nitriding temperature and duration windows.
Outside the optimal processing window, undesirable nitride phases or excessive nitrogen diffusion can reduce the protective effect.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement varies with alloy composition, nitriding temperature, and corrosive environment.
The same corrosion-resistance improvement is not guaranteed across all stainless steel grades.
